The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems: The Architecture of "Hagahot Asheri" and the Shaping of Late Ashkenazi Halakhic Ruling
This article surveys the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems, a key figure in the rehabilitation of the Ashkenazi Torah world after the crises of the 14th century, who served as a bridge between the early traditions of halakhic ruling and practical halakha. The text focuses on his monumental work "Hagahot Asheri", in which he embedded the rulings of the sages of Ashkenaz and Austria into the pages of the Rosh, thereby ensuring the preservation of rare works such as "Sefer Or Zarua" from oblivion. The article stresses how Rabbi Israel's compilatory and concise contribution shaped the infrastructure of late Ashkenazi halakhic ruling, and directly influenced the decisions of the Rema in the Shulchan Arukh. Alongside his halakhic work, his complex public role as **"chief rabbi" on behalf of the Empire** is discussed, an appointment that aroused rabbinic opposition but reflected his standing as a leader navigating between loyalty to tradition and a changing political reality.
The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems: The Architecture of "Hagahot Asheri" and the Shaping of Late Ashkenazi Halakhic Ruling
The Historical and Geopolitical Space of Austrian Jewry in the 14th and 15th Centuries
The historical analysis of the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems requires a deep understanding of the transformations undergone by Ashkenazi Jewry in general, and Austrian Jewry in particular, during the 14th century. This period, marked by recovery from the massacres of the "Black Death" (1348–1349) and from the Rindfleisch massacres that preceded them, was characterized by a significant vacuum of leadership and Torah. The traditional centers of Torah in Germany and France weakened, and the Torah center began to migrate eastward, toward Austria and Bohemia.[1, 2] Rabbi Israel of Krems , who worked in the city of Krems (Krems) on the banks of the Danube, was a key figure in this process of rehabilitation and rebuilding of the world of Ashkenazi halakha.
The city of Krems was at that time an important economic and cultural center in Austria under the rule of the dukes of the House of Habsburg. Its Jewish community was flourishing but subject to unceasing political pressures. Within this reality, Rabbi Israel grew not only into a halakhic decisor and head of a yeshiva, but into a political leader who received official recognition on behalf of the Empire.[3] An understanding of his Torah teaching is not complete without addressing his public roles, since these reflect the dynamic between the internal Torah authority and the external authority of the state.
Rabbi Israel of Krems as "Hochmeister": The Attempt to Establish an Imperial Chief Rabbinate
One of the fascinating and controversial affairs in the life of Rabbi Israel of Krems is his appointment by Emperor Rupert on 3 May 1407 to the position of "Hochmeister" (chief rabbi) over all the Jewish communities in Germany.[3] The imperial decree described Rabbi Israel as a tremendous Torah scholar and "a good man", and granted him Judicial powers and extensive administrative powers. This role included civil control over the Jewish population, supervision of the collection of imperial taxes, and authority to decide internal disputes in the communities.[3]
The rabbinic reaction to this appointment was sharp and unequivocal. The sages of Ashkenaz of that generation saw the appointment of a rabbi on behalf of the foreign government as a mortal blow to communal autonomy and to the foundations of Torah authority, which is not supposed to derive from imperial favor but from the public's inner recognition of the sage's scholarship. The rabbis threatened to impose a ban (cherem) on Rabbi Israel if he exercised his imperial powers, which led to the position becoming to a great extent a dead letter in religious terms, although Rabbi Israel continued to serve in official roles vis-à-vis the government, as attested by a document from 1415 in which he is mentioned as supervising the collection of taxes under Konrad von Weinsberg.[3] This complexity in his figure, as a rabbi accepted by the foreign government but facing internal opposition, perhaps shaped his need to anchor his authority in canonical halakhic writing that would be accepted by the whole of Israel.
Hagahot Asheri: Defining the Genre and the Halakhic Need
The principal work of Rabbi Israel of Krems, known as "Hagahot Asheri", is an exegetical and halakhic work written upon the "Piskei HaRosh" of Rabbeinu Asher ben Yechiel. To understand the importance of the work, one must first understand the standing of the rulings of the Rosh at that time. The Rosh, a disciple of the Maharam of Rothenburg, emigrated from Ashkenaz to Sepharad at the beginning of the 14th century and brought with him the teaching of Ashkenaz and of the Tosafists. In Sepharad, he composed his rulings in a format similar to that of the Rif (Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi), summarizing the Talmudic discussion and deciding the halakha.[4]
However, during the 14th century a gap arose between the rulings of the Rosh in Sepharad and the local traditions of halakhic ruling that continued to develop in Ashkenaz and in Austria. Rabbi Israel of Krems recognized that the Rosh, despite his Ashkenazi origin, did not always include in his rulings the words of the later sages of Ashkenaz or the customs that had crystallized in the communities of Austria and Bohemia.[1, 4] "Hagahot Asheri" was born of the aspiration to bridge this gap and to carry out a renewed "Ashkenazization" of the rulings of the Rosh.
The work is not a continuous commentary but, as its name indicates, a series of short and concise glosses (Glossaries) appearing in the margins of the text of the Rosh. Rabbi Israel works with a methodology of critical compilation: he draws from the sea of the literature of the sages of Ashkenaz the rulings that disagree with the Rosh or complement him, and sets them against him.[4] In this way he turns the "Piskei HaRosh" from a one-dimensional code into a living dialogue between the tradition of Sepharad (represented by the later Rosh) and the original tradition of Ashkenaz.
The Corpus of Sources of Rabbi Israel of Krems and the Preservation of the Teaching of Austria
One of the most significant achievements of Rabbi Israel of Krems is the preservation of halakhic works that were in danger of being lost. In the period before the invention of printing, many books remained in single manuscripts, and whole communities had no access to them. Rabbi Israel held a rich and rare library, and his glosses are based on these sources.[1]
Sefer Or Zarua and Rabbi Yitzchak of Vienna
The most important source in Hagahot Asheri is without doubt "Sefer Or Zarua" by Rabbi Yitzchak of Vienna. The "Or Zarua" is one of the most comprehensive and profound works produced in Ashkenaz in the 13th century, but for historical reasons it did not achieve wide circulation and remained in manuscript until the 19th century.[1, 2] Rabbi Israel of Krems, who worked in the same geographical space as the author of the "Or Zarua", saw in it the supreme source of authority for the customs of Austria.
Through Hagahot Asheri, the rulings of the "Or Zarua" reached the halakhic discussion table of the whole of Israel. Without Rabbi Israel's work of compilation, it is possible that large parts of the teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak of Vienna would have been forgotten entirely. Rabbi Israel not only quoted the "Or Zarua", but often decided in accordance with it against the Rosh, thereby preserving the continuity of early Austrian halakhic ruling.[2]
The Ra'avia and the Mordechai
Other central sources in the work are the books of the Ra'avia (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yoel HaLevi) and the book of the Mordechai (Rabbi Mordechai ben Hillel). While the Rosh often quoted the Ra'avia, Rabbi Israel of Krems brought additional citations that did not appear in the Rosh, especially on matters of local custom and laws dependent on the land in Ashkenaz (such as the laws of prayer and synagogue customs).[2, 4] The book of the Mordechai served him as the halakhic summary of the 14th century, and Rabbi Israel used it to confront the rulings of the Rosh with what had been accepted as binding halakha in Germany.
The Formal Structure of the Work and Its Distribution in the Talmud
Hagahot Asheri covers most of the tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, with an emphasis on tractates that have practical halakhic implications. The work was first printed together with the Piskei HaRosh in the Venice edition of the Talmud (1520–1523) by the printer Daniel Bomberg, and since then it has been an inseparable part of all the standard editions of the Talmud.[1, 4]
Following the order of the tractates reveals the breadth of scope of Rabbi Israel of Krems. He is not content only with the central topics of Choshen Mishpat or Orach Chaim, but penetrates into all areas of halakha.[5, 6]
Details of the Tractates and Orders
In the Order of Moed, his glosses on tractates Shabbat, Eruvin and Pesachim are the most detailed, since these are the areas in which the customs of Ashkenaz differed most significantly from the customs of Sepharad. In the Order of Nashim, he focuses on the laws of betrothal and divorce, with an emphasis on the Ashkenazi "order of the get".[5] In the Order of Nezikin, and especially in tractates Bava Kamma and Bava Metzia, Rabbi Israel incorporates monetary laws based on the economic reality in Austria and Bohemia, such as questions about Jews carrying weapons on the Sabbath in border regions.[2, 5]
This list attests that Rabbi Israel saw his work as a comprehensive code meant to accompany the student and the decisor along the whole Talmudic path. The use of the term "glosses" (Glosses) may mislead and give the work a secondary character, but in practice, for the Jews of Ashkenaz, these glosses were often the bottom line of the halakha.
His Torah Teaching: Halakha, Custom and Society
The Torah teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems is not formulated as philosophical essays; rather, it emerges from his halakhic choices. Several basic principles guiding his writing can be identified:
The Supremacy of Ashkenazi Custom
Rabbi Israel of Krems works out of a deep recognition of the supremacy of early Ashkenazi custom. In his eyes, custom is not merely an addition to halakha, but a source of authority in its own right, at times even against explicit Talmudic proofs.[4] His adherence to sources such as the "Or Zarua" stems from the conception that the tradition passed down from generation to generation in the communities of Ashkenaz is the most precise expression of the will of God. Therefore, when the Rosh in Sepharad rules contrary to this tradition, Rabbi Israel places the gloss in order "to restore the crown to its former glory".
Geopolitical Reality in Halakha
As a leader who was involved in affairs of state, Rabbi Israel did not ignore the surrounding reality. In his work one can find references to the security and economic situations of the Jews of the period. A prominent example is the discussion of whether "our brethren in Bohemia" are permitted to carry weapons on the Sabbath for the purpose of self-defense.[2] Rulings of this kind attest to a realistic rabbinate that understands the needs of the hour and does not shut itself up only within the four cubits of theoretical pilpul. He sees the communities of Bohemia and Austria as one organic unit requiring adapted halakhic solutions.
A Tendency toward Concision and Readability
Unlike the Tosafists, who expanded at length on pilpul and difficulties, Rabbi Israel of Krems prefers the concise style. His glosses are often only a few sentences long, aimed directly at the halakhic conclusion.[4] This style attests to the need of his time for abridgements and practical guides. In the 15th century, the learning public could no longer always encompass the full depth of early Ashkenazi pilpul, and Rabbi Israel provided it with the "refined essence" of the rulings of the Rishonim.[7]
The Krems Dynasty: Rabbi Israel as the Great-Grandfather of the Maharai
It is impossible to discuss the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems without mentioning his influence on one of the greatest decisors of all generations, Rabbi Israel Isserlein, known as the Maharai (author of "Terumat HaDeshen"). Rabbi Israel of Krems was the great-grandfather of the Maharai.[8, 9] The family and Torah connection between the two is a critical component in understanding the development of Ashkenazi halakha.
The Maharai was born around 1390, and grew up within the Torah tradition imparted by his forefather. The Maharai's father, Rabbi Petachiah, was the grandson of Rabbi Israel of Krems.[9] In the works of the Maharai, and especially in "Terumat HaDeshen", one can see how he quotes the rulings of his great-grandfather and uses them as a basis for his own rulings.[3]
The Maharai is regarded as the one who closed the period of the Rishonim in Ashkenaz, and his rulings are based to a great extent on the methodology of Rabbi Israel of Krems: gathering the rulings of the Rishonim, giving decisive weight to local custom, and adapting halakha to the complex reality of life of the Jews of Europe. The name "Israel" given to the Maharai is testimony to the admiration the members of the family felt for the founder of the dynasty in Krems.[9]
The Influence of Hagahot Asheri on Codification: From the Beit Yosef to the Rema
The historical importance of Rabbi Israel of Krems grew in the 16th century, with the beginning of the great process of the codification of halakha. Rabbi Yosef Karo, when he came to compose the "Beit Yosef" and the "Shulchan Arukh", chose the Rosh as one of the three pillars of instruction on which the halakhic ruling rests.[4] Since Hagahot Asheri was printed alongside the Rosh, it was accessible to Rabbi Yosef Karo and served him as a central source for understanding the opinion of the sages of Ashkenaz who disagreed with the Rosh.
However, the most decisive influence of Hagahot Asheri was on Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema). The Rema, who saw himself as continuing the path of the sages of Ashkenaz and Austria, used Hagahot Asheri as an authoritative source of the first rank for writing his glosses on the Shulchan Arukh (the "Mapah").[4, 10]
In many cases in which the Shulchan Arukh ruled in accordance with the Rambam or the Rif, the Rema brought the Ashkenazi custom based on what Rabbi Israel of Krems had written in the name of the "Or Zarua" or the Ra'avia.[10] It can be said that Hagahot Asheri constituted the "raw material" from which the Rema sculpted the Ashkenazi halakhic ruling accepted to this day.
A Synthesis between Sepharad and Ashkenaz
The printed combination of the Rosh (symbolizing the meeting between Ashkenaz and Sepharad) together with Hagahot Asheri (symbolizing pure Ashkenaz) created a complete halakhic product. The student of the Talmud throughout the generations was exposed to both approaches simultaneously. This influence is also evident in later commentaries on the Rosh, such as the "Ma'adanei Yom Tov" and the "Pilpula Charifta" of Rabbi Yom Tov Lipmann Heller, and the "Korban Netanel" of Rabbi Netanel Weil, all of which treated Hagahot Asheri as a canonical text requiring attention.[11]
An In-Depth Analysis: Hagahot Asheri as a Bridge between Generations
In a broad view, the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems exemplifies the mechanism of "preservation through annotation". In the history of Jewish literature, it is at times precisely the texts written as "glosses" or as "footnotes" that have preserved the deepest traditional heritage. Rabbi Israel did not try to replace the Rosh, but to live within him and beside him. This is an expression of scholarly humility on the one hand, but also of self-confidence in the Ashkenazi tradition on the other.
He understood that in the changing world of the 15th century, the survival of the teaching of Ashkenaz depended on its ability to become integrated into the central Talmudic canon. By attaching the words of the "Or Zarua" and the Ra'avia to the rulings of the Rosh, he ensured that these sources would not remain the possession of a few individuals in Austria, but would become the possession of all.[1]
Facing the Challenges of Early Modernity
Although Rabbi Israel worked at the close of the Middle Ages, his teaching carries within it the buds of modernity. His need to organize halakha in an accessible form, his use of diverse sources, and his recognition of political authority all herald the figure of the rabbi in the early modern era. He is not only a "Torah scholar" but also an "editor" and a "disseminator", a figure mediating between hidden knowledge and a public thirsting for clear ways of life.
Conclusions and Summary Insights on the Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems
The study of the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems reveals a picture of a multidimensional figure who influenced the shaping of halakha for generations. His Torah teaching, embodied in "Hagahot Asheri", is one of the most important junctions in the development of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling.
The key points of his contribution can be summarized as follows:
Preservation and rescue: he served as a "living archive" for the teaching of the early sages of Ashkenaz and Austria, foremost among them the "Or Zarua", and thereby prevented the loss of central rulings and customs.[1, 2]
Canonical bridging: he created a synthesis between the rulings of the Rosh and the tradition of Ashkenaz, which enabled European Jewry to continue using the work of the Rosh without giving up its distinctive identity.[4]
Long-term influence: his rulings and glosses formed the infrastructure on which the Rema's "Mapah" was built, and thereby influenced the way of life of millions of Jews over hundreds of years.[4, 10]
Complex leadership: his figure as "Hochmeister" and as a public leader teaches of the early attempts of Ashkenazi Jewry to navigate between halakhic loyalty and integration into the systems of imperial government.[3]
Rabbi Israel of Krems remains to this day one of the heroes of the spiritual culture of Ashkenaz. His glosses, printed permanently in the margins of the Talmud, are a constant reminder that halakha is a dynamic creation, built out of a dialogue between generations, between geographical centers and between custom and text. His family, and especially his great-grandson the Maharai, continued in his path and made the legacy of Krems the backbone of the world of halakha to this very day.[8, 9]

Hagahot Asheri covers most of the tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, with an emphasis on tractates that have practical halakhic implications. The work was first printed together with the Piskei HaRosh in the Venice edition of the Talmud (1520–1523) by the printer Daniel Bomberg, and since then it has been an inseparable part of all the standard editions of the Talmud.[1, 4]

Details of the Tractates and Orders
In the Order of Moed, his glosses on tractates Shabbat, Eruvin and Pesachim are the most detailed, since these are the areas in which the customs of Ashkenaz differed most significantly from the customs of Sepharad. The Torah teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems is not formulated as philosophical essays; rather, it emerges from his halakhic choices. Several basic principles guiding his writing can be identified:

It is impossible to discuss the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems without mentioning his influence on one of the greatest decisors of all generations, Rabbi Israel Isserlein, known as the Maharai (author of "Terumat HaDeshen"). The Maharai was born around 1390, and grew up within the Torah tradition imparted by his forefather. The Maharai is regarded as the one who closed the period of the Rishonim in Ashkenaz, and his rulings are based to a great extent on the methodology of Rabbi Israel of Krems: gathering the rulings of the Rishonim, giving decisive weight to local custom, and adapting halakha to the complex reality of life of the Jews of Europe. The historical importance of Rabbi Israel of Krems grew in the 16th century, with the beginning of the great process of the codification of halakha. The printed combination of the Rosh (symbolizing the meeting between Ashkenaz and Sepharad) together with Hagahot Asheri (symbolizing pure Ashkenaz) created a complete halakhic product. In a broad view, the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems exemplifies the mechanism of "preservation through annotation". In the history of Jewish literature, it is at times precisely the texts written as "glosses" or as "footnotes" that have preserved the deepest traditional heritage. Rabbi Israel did not try to replace the Rosh, but to live within him and beside him. This is an expression of scholarly humility on the one hand, but also of self-confidence in the Ashkenazi tradition on the other.

By attaching the words of the "Or Zarua" and the Ra'avia to the rulings of the Rosh, he ensured that these sources would not remain the possession of a few individuals in Austria, but would become the possession of all.[1]
Facing the Challenges of Early Modernity
Although Rabbi Israel worked at the close of the Middle Ages, his teaching carries within it the buds of modernity. His need to organize halakha in an accessible form, his use of diverse sources, and his recognition of political authority all herald the figure of the rabbi in the early modern era. He is not only a "Torah scholar" but also an "editor" and a "disseminator", a figure mediating between hidden knowledge and a public thirsting for clear ways of life.
Conclusions and Summary Insights on the Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems
The study of the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems reveals a picture of a multidimensional figure who influenced the shaping of halakha for generations. His Torah teaching, embodied in "Hagahot Asheri", is one of the most important junctions in the development of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling.
The key points of his contribution can be summarized as follows:
Preservation and rescue: he served as a "living archive" for the teaching of the early sages of Ashkenaz and Austria, foremost among them the "Or Zarua", and thereby prevented the loss of central rulings and customs.[1, 2]
Canonical bridging: he created a synthesis between the rulings of the Rosh and the tradition of Ashkenaz, which enabled European Jewry to continue using the work of the Rosh without giving up its distinctive identity.[4]
Long-term influence: his rulings and glosses formed the infrastructure on which the Rema's "Mapah" was built, and thereby influenced the way of life of millions of Jews over hundreds of years.[4, 10]
Complex leadership: his figure as "Hochmeister" and as a public leader teaches of the early attempts of Ashkenazi Jewry to navigate between halakhic loyalty and integration into the systems of imperial government.[3]
Rabbi Israel of Krems remains to this day one of the heroes of the spiritual culture of Ashkenaz. His glosses, printed permanently in the margins of the Talmud, are a constant reminder that halakha is a dynamic creation, built out of a dialogue between generations, between geographical centers and between custom and text. His family, and especially his great-grandson the Maharai, continued in his path and made the legacy of Krems the backbone of the world of halakha to this very day.[8, 9]

The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems: The Architecture of "Hagahot Asheri" and the Shaping of Late Ashkenazi Halakhic Ruling
This article surveys the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems, a key figure in the rehabilitation of the Ashkenazi Torah world after the crises of the 14th century, who served as a bridge between the early traditions of halakhic ruling and practical halakha. The text focuses on his monumental work "Hagahot Asheri", in which he embedded the rulings of the sages of Ashkenaz and Austria into the pages of the Rosh, thereby ensuring the preservation of rare works such as "Sefer Or Zarua" from oblivion. The article stresses how Rabbi Israel's compilatory and concise contribution shaped the infrastructure of late Ashkenazi halakhic ruling, and directly influenced the decisions of the Rema in the Shulchan Arukh. Alongside his halakhic work, his complex public role as **"chief rabbi" on behalf of the Empire** is discussed, an appointment that aroused rabbinic opposition but reflected his standing as a leader navigating between loyalty to tradition and a changing political reality.

The Historical and Geopolitical Space of Austrian Jewry in the 14th and 15th Centuries
The historical analysis of the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems requires a deep understanding of the transformations undergone by Ashkenazi Jewry in general, and Austrian Jewry in particular, during the 14th century. This period, marked by recovery from the massacres of the "Black Death" (1348–1349) and from the Rindfleisch massacres that preceded them, was characterized by a significant vacuum of leadership and Torah. The traditional centers of Torah in Germany and France weakened, and the Torah center began to migrate eastward, toward Austria and Bohemia.[1, 2] Rabbi Israel of Krems , who worked in the city of Krems (Krems) on the banks of the Danube, was a key figure in this process of rehabilitation and rebuilding of the world of Ashkenazi halakha.
The city of Krems was at that time an important economic and cultural center in Austria under the rule of the dukes of the House of Habsburg. Its Jewish community was flourishing but subject to unceasing political pressures. Within this reality, Rabbi Israel grew not only into a halakhic decisor and head of a yeshiva, but into a political leader who received official recognition on behalf of the Empire.[3] An understanding of his Torah teaching is not complete without addressing his public roles, since these reflect the dynamic between the internal Torah authority and the external authority of the state.
Rabbi Israel of Krems as "Hochmeister": The Attempt to Establish an Imperial Chief Rabbinate
One of the fascinating and controversial affairs in the life of Rabbi Israel of Krems is his appointment by Emperor Rupert on 3 May 1407 to the position of "Hochmeister" (chief rabbi) over all the Jewish communities in Germany.[3] The imperial decree described Rabbi Israel as a tremendous Torah scholar and "a good man", and granted him Judicial powers and extensive administrative powers. This role included civil control over the Jewish population, supervision of the collection of imperial taxes, and authority to decide internal disputes in the communities.[3]
The rabbinic reaction to this appointment was sharp and unequivocal. The sages of Ashkenaz of that generation saw the appointment of a rabbi on behalf of the foreign government as a mortal blow to communal autonomy and to the foundations of Torah authority, which is not supposed to derive from imperial favor but from the public's inner recognition of the sage's scholarship. The rabbis threatened to impose a ban (cherem) on Rabbi Israel if he exercised his imperial powers, which led to the position becoming to a great extent a dead letter in religious terms, although Rabbi Israel continued to serve in official roles vis-à-vis the government, as attested by a document from 1415 in which he is mentioned as supervising the collection of taxes under Konrad von Weinsberg.[3] This complexity in his figure, as a rabbi accepted by the foreign government but facing internal opposition, perhaps shaped his need to anchor his authority in canonical halakhic writing that would be accepted by the whole of Israel.
Hagahot Asheri: Defining the Genre and the Halakhic Need
The principal work of Rabbi Israel of Krems, known as "Hagahot Asheri", is an exegetical and halakhic work written upon the "Piskei HaRosh" of Rabbeinu Asher ben Yechiel. The Rosh, a disciple of the Maharam of Rothenburg, emigrated from Ashkenaz to Sepharad at the beginning of the 14th century and brought with him the teaching of Ashkenaz and of the Tosafists. In Sepharad, he composed his rulings in a format similar to that of the Rif (Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi), summarizing the Talmudic discussion and deciding the halakha.[4]
However, during the 14th century a gap arose between the rulings of the Rosh in Sepharad and the local traditions of halakhic ruling that continued to develop in Ashkenaz and in Austria. Rabbi Israel of Krems recognized that the Rosh, despite his Ashkenazi origin, did not always include in his rulings the words of the later sages of Ashkenaz or the customs that had crystallized in the communities of Austria and Bohemia.[1, 4] "Hagahot Asheri" was born of the aspiration to bridge this gap and to carry out a renewed "Ashkenazization" of the rulings of the Rosh.
The work is not a continuous commentary but, as its name indicates, a series of short and concise glosses (Glossaries) appearing in the margins of the text of the Rosh. Rabbi Israel works with a methodology of critical compilation: he draws from the sea of the literature of the sages of Ashkenaz the rulings that disagree with the Rosh or complement him, and sets them against him.[4] In this way he turns the "Piskei HaRosh" from a one-dimensional code into a living dialogue between the tradition of Sepharad (represented by the later Rosh) and the original tradition of Ashkenaz.

One of the most significant achievements of Rabbi Israel of Krems is the preservation of halakhic works that were in danger of being lost. In the period before the invention of printing, many books remained in single manuscripts, and whole communities had no access to them. Rabbi Israel held a rich and rare library, and his glosses are based on these sources.[1]

Conclusions and Summary Insights on the Teaching of Rabbi Israel of Krems
The study of the work of Rabbi Israel of Krems reveals a picture of a multidimensional figure who influenced the shaping of halakha for generations. His Torah teaching, embodied in "Hagahot Asheri", is one of the most important junctions in the development of Ashkenazi halakhic ruling.
The key points of his contribution can be summarized as follows:
Preservation and rescue: he served as a "living archive" for the teaching of the early sages of Ashkenaz and Austria, foremost among them the "Or Zarua", and thereby prevented the loss of central rulings and customs.[1, 2]
Canonical bridging: he created a synthesis between the rulings of the Rosh and the tradition of Ashkenaz, which enabled European Jewry to continue using the work of the Rosh without giving up its distinctive identity.[4]
Long-term influence: his rulings and glosses formed the infrastructure on which the Rema's "Mapah" was built, and thereby influenced the way of life of millions of Jews over hundreds of years.[4, 10]
Complex leadership: his figure as "Hochmeister" and as a public leader teaches of the early attempts of Ashkenazi Jewry to navigate between halakhic loyalty and integration into the systems of imperial government.[3]
Rabbi Israel of Krems remains to this day one of the heroes of the spiritual culture of Ashkenaz. His glosses, printed permanently in the margins of the Talmud, are a constant reminder that halakha is a dynamic creation, built out of a dialogue between generations, between geographical centers and between custom and text. His family, and especially his great-grandson the Maharai, continued in his path and made the legacy of Krems the backbone of the world of halakha to this very day.[8, 9]
